title: Comfort, lived
hook: the Shabbat after Tisha B'Av, "Comfort ye", begins seven weeks of comfort
tomorrow: who decides what goes on your calendar?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tisha B'Av: on the floor with Lamentations until midday. Sit low. Then the calendar turns, sooner than you might expect.

When someone you love is grieving, the hardest part is often the first sentence. Everything you draft sounds wrong. So what does the prophet say first, on the Shabbat after the floor? Two words, and then the same two again: "Comfort ye, comfort ye My people, saith your God." That Shabbat is called Shabbat Nachamu, the Shabbat of comfort, after the first word of its reading from Isaiah. And the comfort doesn't stop after one week.
screen: `THE HARDEST FIRST SENTENCE.` → `COMFORT YE, COMFORT YE.` → `SHABBAT NACHAMU.`

segments.voice: After Tisha B'Av come seven Shabbatot of comfort readings from Isaiah, leading toward Rosh Hashanah. The sorrow gets a day; the comfort gets a season. And notice the doubling: comfort ye, comfort ye. Some readers hear comfort that has to be said more than once, because grief doesn't hear it the first time. The tradition also teaches how to comfort one person, not only a people. When Job's friends hear of his losses, they come and sit with him on the ground, and the text says "none spoke a word unto him; for they saw that his grief was very great." The Talmud draws a rule from visits like that: those who come to comfort a mourner don't speak until the mourner speaks first. Comfort starts as presence. Words come second, and they follow the grieving person's lead. When visitors leave a house of mourning, there's a traditional line for the mourner: may God comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. The private loss is held inside a larger one, also waiting for comfort. So comfort, lived, is small: show up, sit down, let them speak first, and keep coming back for weeks, not only the first day.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person carrying something heavy right now. Write a short text you could send them, just a few words, with no advice in it at all: only that you're thinking of them, or that you're there. Read it once, slowly, and decide when it should go.

segments.voice: Shabbat Nachamu: the Shabbat of comfort after Tisha B'Av, named for Isaiah's first words, comfort ye, comfort ye.
A line to carry: comfort follows, slowly, and it usually starts by sitting down. Until next time.
